With the continuous expansion of the digital domain and the increasing need for higher chip integration, quantum-dot cellular
automata (QCA) has emerged as a promising alternative to CMOS technology. However, existing QCA designs often face
signifcant challenges, including high delay, large area, and inefcient wire crossing techniques, which limit their practical
applicability. Tis paper addresses these gaps by proposing novel two-bit and four-bit multiplier designs that leverage efcient
adder blocks and innovative coplanar wire crossing strategies. Our work introduces eight key design guidelines derived through
extensive simulation and experimentation in the QCADesigner. Tese guidelines address critical challenges in the QCA circuit
design, such as signal propagation, clocking, and interference minimization, ensuring reliable logic transmission and improved
circuit performance. Te proposed single-layer multipliers demonstrate signifcant improvements over existing designs, with
a 65% reduction in delay, a 43% reduction in area, and a 39% reduction in cell count for the two-bit multiplier. For the four-bit
multiplier, improvements of 32.5% in delay, 48% in area, and 28% in cell count are achieved. In comparison with multilayer
designs, our two-bit multiplier achieves similar delay performance while ofering 16% and 31% improvements in area and cell
count, respectively. Although the four-bit multiplier shows an increase in area, cell count, and delay compared to multilayer
designs, it remains the most efcient single-layer implementation to date. Te proposed designs not only advance the state-of-
the-art in QCA multipliers but also provide a scalable framework for future research in high-speed, low-power digital circuits. Tis
work highlights the importance of systematic design methodologies in QCA technology and paves the way for more efcient and
reliable nanoscale computing systems.
Keywords: adder; coplanar design; high-speed multiplier; quantum-dot cellular automata (QCA); wire crossing
1. Introduction
Te increasing demand for enhanced chip integration and
the constraints of transistor miniaturization have led to
a growing interest in quantum-dot cellular automata (QCA)
as a potential alternative to CMOS technology for digital
circuit design. With its distinctive features, such as high
speed, reduced energy consumption, and lower density
compared to CMOS, QCA is positioned as a promising
candidate for future high-performance electronic applica-
tions like mobile devices and autonomous systems. Te
technology also ofers opportunities for optimized circuit
designs with reduced cell count and wire crossovers, leading
to improved circuit performance. Recent advancements in
QCA design have been signifcant, as evidenced by nu-
merous publications in 2024 [1–6]. Tese studies have
demonstrated the growing interest and potential of QCA
technology in various applications. Furthermore, a recent
fabrication study in reference [3] highlights the ongoing
research eforts in materials science and chemistry to further
develop QCA devices, suggesting a promising future for this
emerging feld.
Designing multipliers is crucial in the design of digital
circuits, especially in the realm of QCA technology. Efcient
multiplier designs in QCA can utilize the technology’s high
speed

Tis paper presents new multiplier designs with im-
proved circuit parameters compared to previous designs,
including two new two-bit and two new four-bit multipliers
that demonstrate signifcant enhancements in delay, area,
and cell count. In this work, we introduce eight key design
guidelines that address critical challenges in the QCA circuit
design, such as signal propagation, clocking, and wire
crossing. Tese guidelines were derived through extensive
simulation and experimentation in the QCADesigner,
building on the limitations of traditional QCA design
methods. While conventional approaches rely on changing
the clock phase at each logic gate, modern designs often use
innovative techniques that lack a clear theoretical founda-
tion.
Our
guidelines,
however,
provide
a
systematic
framework for designing reliable and scalable QCA circuits.
Tey are based on the principle that the efective feld of
a quantum cell has a limited range and any overlap with
neighboring cells can disrupt logic operations. By carefully
arranging cells, optimizing clocking schemes, and mini-
mizing interference, these guidelines ensure correct logic
propagation and improve circuit performance. Importantly,
these principles are not limited to multiplier circuits; they
can be applied to a wide range of QCA designs, including
adders, multiplexers, and memory units. A detailed dis-
cussion of these guidelines and their application is provided
in Section 4. Tese advancements signify a notable progress
in the feld of QCA multipliers, ofering promising prospects
for enhanced computational performance and efciency in
digital systems. Te main contributions of this paper
included:
• Enhanced Safoev and Ahmed full adders (FAs): We
have modifed the Safoev and Ahmed designs to ac-
commodate larger circuits (four-bit) through opti-
mized clocking. For smaller circuits (two-bit), the
original Safoev and Ahmed designs were sufcient.
• Novel hybrid routing strategy: Unlike traditional phase
rotation and phase inversion techniques, we propose
a hybrid routing method that ensures both reliable
logic propagation and stability in long wires, which is
crucial for larger circuits.
• Fastest and most efcient QCA multiplier: Tis paper
introduces the fastest coplanar QCA multiplier with
the lowest cell count.
• Comprehensive design guidelines: We have extracted
and articulated eight key design guidelines that can
serve as a blueprint for designing QCA circuits across
various applications.
Te structure of the remaining sections in this paper is as
follows: the following section encompasses QCA funda-
mentals. Subsequently, a review of related work and the
motivation behind this study is provided. Section 4 delves
into the discussion of the proposed novel multipliers.
Simulation results and discussions are detailed in Section 5,
culminating in the conclusion in Section 6.
2. QCA Preliminaries
QCA represents a groundbreaking nanotechnology that
enables the implementation of digital logic at the molecular
scale. QCA leverages Coulombic interactions between
quantum dots to encode and process information. Key
components of QCA include:
• QCA Cells: Tese are the fundamental building blocks
of QCA circuits, consisting of an array of quantum
dots arranged in a grid pattern. Electrons tunnel be-
tween these dots to represent binary values.
• Clocking: Synchronization is crucial for the reliable
operation of QCA circuits. Techniques like clock-zone
assignment and clock phase separation are employed
to mitigate clock skew.
• Wire Crossing: Coplanar crossover is a common
method for crossing wires in QCA circuits, mini-
mizing signal distortion.
• Coplanar versus Multilayer Designs: In QCA tech-
nology, circuits can be implemented in two main
confgurations: coplanar and multilayer. A coplanar
design refers to a circuit where all quantum cells are
placed on a single layer. Tis approach simplifes
fabrication and is more feasible with the current
technology. However, coplanar designs face chal-
lenges such as signal interference and wire crossing
issues. In contrast, multilayer designs involve stacking
cells in multiple layers, which allows for more com-
plex and compact circuits. However, multilayer de-
signs
are
currently
not
feasible
for
practical
implementation because of fabrication limitations. In
this work, we focus on coplanar designs to ensure that
our proposed multipliers can be implemented in real-
world applications.
• MV Gates: MV gates are a type of logic gate in QCA
used for implementing basic logic functions such as
AND, OR, and NOT.
Figure 1 illustrates some of these key concepts in QCA
technology. For a comprehensive understanding of QCA
and its circuit design principles, readers are encouraged to
refer to references [7, 8]. Tese references provide detailed
discussions on QCA technology and its applications.
Utilizing tools such as the QCADesigner and QCAPro
greatly facilitates the design, simulation, and optimization of
QCA circuits. While the QCADesigner is commonly used
for conventional design and simulation tasks, direct power
consumption calculations using this software can be limited.
To overcome this limitation, two alternative software so-
lutions have been developed: QCADesigner Pro and
QCADesigner E (Energy). Tese tools ofer enhanced ca-
pabilities for extracting power consumption data from
quantum circuits efciently. In this study, the QCADesigner
E software was specifcally employed for power consumption

3. Related Works
Various multiplier architectures have been proposed over
the years, each with its own advantages and disadvantages.
Common types include Array Multiplier, Wallace Tree
Multiplier, Dadda Multiplier, Booth Multiplier, Modifed
Booth Multiplier, Carry-Save Multiplier, and so on. Tey
provide trade-ofs among speed, area, and power. While
CMOS technology has provided us with a rich variety of
multiplier architectures, the emerging QCA technology
ofers new possibilities. Although the nomenclature of
multiplier designs in QCA often mirrors that of CMOS, it’s
crucial to recognize that direct comparisons are not always
straightforward. A multiplier that exhibits high speed in
CMOS might not perform as well in QCA because of the
unique properties of quantum-dot cells. Subsequently, we
will explore the QCA multiplier designs presented in the
literature. Tese designs will be instrumental in our com-
parative analysis, allowing us to evaluate the performance of
the proposed multipliers and draw meaningful conclusions.
In 2003, Walus et al. from the University of British
Columbia, Canada presented a two-bit serial-parallel multi-
plier architecture in paper [9]. Tis design utilized two one-bit
adders with shifting capabilities to perform multiplication of
two two-bit operands. Notably, this design was among the
most optimized single-layer implementations of its time.
However, a primary limitation was its substantial delay. In
addition, as outputs were generated asynchronously, the
absence of dedicated output storage or registers hindered
result capture at specifc clock cycles. In the realm of serial
multipliers, reference [10] in 2021 introduced a serial-parallel
multiplier with enhanced reliability, capable of handling
larger bit-width operands. Te multiplier employs local QCA
registers to temporarily store input bits before multiplication,
thereby improving data retention and reliability.
Hanninen and Takala [11] in 2007 presented a com-
prehensive pipelined parallel array multiplier. Te proposed
design implemented a three-bit array multiplier using
a single-layer layout with coplanar wiring. Both inputs and
outputs were fully parallel. Te multiplier employed
a Hanninen FA, as described in reference [12]. Te Han-
ninen adder required one clock cycle delay for carry gen-
eration and two clock cycle delays for sum generation.
In 2010, Kim and Swartzlander presented a four-bit and
eight-bit array multiplier design in reference [13]. All
proposed designs in this reference were implemented using
a single-layer layout with coplanar wiring. Tese structures
were based on ripple-carry propagation and exhibited
a highly regular layout.
Yang and Afrooz [14] proposed new two-bit array
multiplier designs in 2019. Te main goal was to improve
upon existing designs. Te FA used in this multiplier was
adapted from reference [15]. A four-bit Wallace multiplier
design was introduced in reference [16]. Tis design
employed a multilayer structure with noncoplanar cross-
overs. While the implementation was optimized in terms of
cell count and area, it sufered from signifcant delay.
Subsequently, in 2020, reference [17] presented an improved
four-bit Wallace multiplier design. Similar to reference [16],
this design utilized a multilayer structure with noncoplanar
crossovers. However, it ofered several optimizations com-
pared to the previous design. If you’ve noticed, Wallace
multipliers implemented in recent years have been pre-
dominantly multilayer. To fnd a single-layer implementa-
tion of a Wallace multiplier, reference [18] can be cited.
Advanced array multipliers, such as the Baugh–Wooley
multiplier, have been extensively studied. Te Baugh–Wooley
multiplier is a notable example of array multipliers. Reference

plored both coplanar and multilayer implementations of sys-

coplanar and multilayer routing. A Vedic multiplier designed
for four-bit multiplication was proposed in reference [22].
Unlike previous designs, this multiplier employed a carry-save
adder (CSA) structure. Te QCA implementation adopted
a multilayer structure with noncoplanar crossovers. In 2020,
reference [23] introduced a high-speed Vedic multiplier design,
also implemented using a multilayer structure.
A groundbreaking advancement in high-speed array
multiplier design was achieved in 2023. Yan et al. [4] pre-
sented record-breaking two-bit and three-bit array multi-
pliers, utilizing the innovative XOR gate-based structure of
the Gassoumi adder introduced in [24]. Given its speed, the
Gassoumi adder was an excellent choice for multiplier
implementation, as demonstrated by Yan’s design. However,
despite its advantages, a major drawback of the design in [4]
is its multilayer implementation. As it is well-known,
multilayer designs are currently not feasible for hardware
implementation and are limited to simulations. Another
limitation of this design is the irregular pattern of input and
output signals, requiring modifcations for large-scale
implementations.
Recent advancements in QCA-based multipliers have
focused on improving energy efciency, scalability, and
fault tolerance. For instance, Ahmadpour et al. [25] pro-
posed a novel energy-efcient quantum-based multiplier
for nanoscale IoT devices, addressing the limitations of
previous designs in terms of speed, area, and energy
consumption. Teir work introduced innovative quantum-
based adders and demonstrated signifcant improvements
in energy efciency and occupied area. Similarly, Daggula
and Bevara [26] presented an ultra-low power QCA-based
Vedic multiplier for digital radar applications, achieving
remarkable reductions in power consumption and area
while maintaining high performance. Teir design utilized
only 2940 cells and occupied 7.33 μm2, making it highly
suitable for real-time phased array radar systems. In an-
other study, Das and De [27] proposed a four-bit multiplier
using a CSA in QCA technology, focusing on reducing cell
count and clock delay. Teir design outperformed previous
architectures in terms of efciency and scalability. In ad-
dition, Gladshtein [28] introduced a novel QCA serial
decimal digit multiplier, leveraging the unique properties
of QCA wires for serial data processing. Tis design showed
signifcant hardware simplifcation compared to traditional
BCD multipliers, making it a promising approach for fu-
ture computing facilities. Furthermore, Seyedi and Abdoli
[29] addressed the critical issue of fault tolerance in QCA
circuits by proposing a fault-tolerant CSA for IoT devices.
Teir design demonstrated an 85% tolerance for diferent
types of failures, making it highly reliable for applications
requiring continuous operation in fault-prone environ-
ments. Tese recent works highlight the ongoing eforts to
overcome the challenges of QCA technology, paving the
way for more efcient and reliable nanoscale computing
systems.
4. Proposed Multiplier
In this section, we introduce novel two-bit and four-bit array
multiplier architectures. Te proposed multipliers operate
on unsigned integers. Notably, two types of multipliers are
presented in this paper. Te frst multiplier utilizes a mod-
ifed version of the FA proposed in reference [4], while the
second multiplier employs the FA design presented in
reference [6]. A detailed comparison between the proposed
designs and previous works will be provided in a subsequent
section. As is well-known, previous QCA multiplier designs
have been implemented in both single-layer and multilayer
confgurations. While both approaches have been explored
in various research, the signifcant challenge lies in the
fabrication limitations of multilayer QCA designs. To date,
only single-layer QCA designs have been experimentally
realized.
Consequently,
our
proposed
multipliers
are
implemented in a single-layer (coplanar) confguration,
enabling potential hardware testing and implementation in
the future.
Prior to presenting the detailed designs, it is crucial to
discuss key concepts related to coplanar routing and the
proper use of clock phases for reliable polarity transfer in
long wires. Tese fundamental principles underpin our
proposed designs and are essential for understanding the
subsequent discussions.
4.1. Introduction of New Concepts in the QCA Circuit Design.
Te frst novel aspect of our proposed architectures involves
a hybrid approach to wire crossing. Traditionally, coplanar
wire crossings in QCA are achieved in two ways: (a) using
wires in diferent phases and (b) using 45-degree rotated
cells. In this paper, we introduce a hybrid crossing method
that combines these two conventional approaches. Specif-
cally, coplanar crossings are achieved using rotated cells in
diferent phases. While this combination limits the number
of possible crossing confgurations (as illustrated in Fig-
ure 2), it signifcantly enhances the reliability and efciency
of long-wire routing, facilitating logic transmission.
A second key innovation in our proposed designs is the
meticulous evaluation of the electromagnetic energy levels
within cells in long wires. Fundamental studies in the QCA
circuit design indicate that for highly reliable logic trans-
mission, a continuous phase shift between adjacent cells is
optimal. However, this continuous phase shift can introduce
signifcant delays in large circuits. Consequently, a de facto
design rule has emerged in recent designs to avoid sequential
phase shifts, thereby reducing delay. Unfortunately, this
practice can compromise the certainty of the fnal output,
and simulations may not consistently reproduce the original
circuit behavior. Accurate results often require fne-tuning
of simulation parameters such as polarization, cell size, and
other quantum cell characteristics. Given these challenges,
we have conducted a more in-depth analysis of this issue.
Our fndings reveal that in long wires, there is a consistent
decrease in the electromagnetic energy holding electrons
within cells (i.e., the determined polarity). Consequently,
when transmitting polarity through a long wire using

4.2. Proposed Multipliers. We begin by introducing the
Type-I two-bit multiplier. A comprehensive theoretical
analysis and detailed design of this multiplier are presented
in this section. To avoid redundancy, a detailed description
of the Type-II structure and four-bit multipliers is omitted.
In an unsigned two-bit array multiplier with inputs A (a0,
a1) and B (b0, b1), the fnal product is obtained by summing
the partial products (PPs). To realize this structure in QCA,
designers must innovate in two critical areas to optimize cell
count, delay, area, and power consumption: the selection of
fundamental building blocks and the confguration of
interconnections.
Te fundamental building blocks are the AND gate and the
FA. Following previous research, we employ a majority voter
(MV) to implement the AND gate. By setting one input of the
MV to a constant “1,” it functions as an AND gate. For the FA,
the Safoev adder [30], one of the most efcient adders in recent
years, is adopted. Tis adder ofers an optimal balance of circuit
characteristics (delay, cell count, and area) and a well-organized
cell arrangement. Tis arrangement ensures that inputs and
outputs are readily accessible, making it suitable for large-scale
circuits like multipliers.
However, because of polarity uncertainties in larger
circuits, the Safoev adder failed to provide the required
performance. Tis issue was resolved by modifying the phase
arrangement of the quantum cells. Te modifed Safoev
adder structure is depicted in Figure 3.
Interconnections and wiring between blocks require
meticulous attention. Design in this area necessitates con-
sidering numerous factors and making complex trade-ofs.
While the power-speed trade-of is well-understood in the
CMOS design, QCA presents a new challenge: a trade-of
between circuit parameters (delay, cell count, and area) and
quantum cell polarization. Higher polarization enhances the
reliability of logic transmission but often leads to increased
delay and reduced density. Optimal QCA design requires
designers to efciently propagate logic signals with the
lowest possible polarization level. Figures 4 and 5 present
our proposed two-bit multiplier design that addresses this
challenge. In the following, we provide a detailed exposition
of the design, including the rationale behind the architec-
tural choices.
In the following, we delve into the intricate design
considerations employed in the proposed QCA layout, as
illustrated in Figure 6.
1. Wire Branching: A common technique for branching
from a standard wire is demonstrated. While initial
intuition suggested that phase shifting might not be
necessary at such junctions, rigorous simulations
revealed that separating at least two in-phase cells
from the main wire before introducing a phase shift is
essential for mitigating refections.
2. Rotated Wire Branching: Branching from rotated
wires is achieved by vertically shifting the adjacent cell
by 9 nm. Te inherent nature of rotated wires allows
for both the original and inverted signals to be ob-
tained from the branch. Careful selection of the
shifted cell’s position is crucial to ensure that the
correct input is branched.
3. Cell Rotation (45-Degree) for Wire Crossing: Tis
method is particularly efective in regions near inputs
because of the higher certainty and robustness of cell
polarization in these areas.
4. Phase Shift (90-Degree) for Wire Crossing: Suitable
for intermediate data transmission, this method is
employed extensively to reduce the layout area
compared to the 45-degree rotation method.
5. Hybrid Crossing Method: A novel hybrid crossing
method is introduced for regions with high cell
density or where wires are frequently interrupted. Tis
method combines the advantages of the previous two
approaches.
6. Cell Spacing: A minimum spacing of two cells or
36 nm is maintained between wires to ensure reliable

We introduce two novel two-bit multiplier designs,

5. Results and Discussion
In this section, a comparison between the proposed mul-
tipliers and existing designs is presented. Te proposed
designs are validated using QCADesigner version 2.0.3, and
QCADesigner-E is used for the measurement of power
consumption. To enable comparison, some of the best
previous multipliers have been selected. Evaluation pa-
rameters include cell count, latency, area, and power con-
sumption. It is worth noting that some references do not
report power consumption, thus the power comparison
table is somewhat incomplete.
Simulation results for the proposed Type-I and Type-II

A comparison between the proposed designs and
existing works is presented in this section to highlight their
strengths and weaknesses. Tis section can be divided into
subsections for two-bit and four-bit multipliers. A com-
prehensive comparison is conducted based on results
obtained from both proposed and previous designs. For
a fair comparison, standardized criteria have been selected.
Considering the classifcation of QCA designs into single-
layer and multilayer, this factor has been a primary con-
sideration. In addition, the type of multiplier architecture
(e.g., array, Vedic, and Wallace) has been taken into ac-
count because of its impact on comparison metrics. Given
our focus on high-speed, single-layer, unsigned array
multipliers, the primary comparison is against previous
single-layer array designs. However, to provide a broader
perspective and showcase the improvements of the pro-
posed designs, results from multilayer multipliers with
diferent architectures have also been included.
Table 1 presents the circuit parameters of various two-bit
multipliers. Te comparison criteria in this table include: the
number of quantum cells, the occupied area in square
micrometers, the delay in terms of clock cycles, and the
implementation method as single-layer (Coplanar) or
multilayer (M). Te multipliers listed in Table 1 are cate-
gorized into two main groups: multilayer and single-layer
designs, from top to bottom, respectively. Undoubtedly,
multilayer designs ofer more design fexibility and often
allow for better designs. However, the inability to fabricate
multilayer designs is the main obstacle for the development
of such designs. Terefore, our focus has been on the single-
layer design. A fair comparison would be to compare the
proposed designs in this thesis with single-layer designs.
A comparison of the proposed designs with previous
works is presented. Table 1 shows that the proposed Type-I
design outperforms the fastest single-layer design [14] by
20%, 23%, and 23% in terms of delay, area, and cell count,
respectively. However, when compared to the multilayer
reference design [4], the proposed design exhibits only a 14%
improvement in cell count, while experiencing a 65% in-
crease in delay and a 10% increase in area. Despite this, the
proposed Type-I design represents a signifcant advance-
ment in single-layer designs.
Te proposed Type-II multiplier demonstrates signif-
cant improvements compared to previous designs. As shown
in Table 1, it achieves a 65%, 43%, and 39% reduction in
delay, area, and cell count, respectively, compared to the best
single-layer design [14]. When compared to multilayer
designs, the proposed design ofers a 16% and 31% reduction
in area and cell count, respectively, while maintaining
a comparable delay to the best multilayer design [4]. Given
the challenges in fabricating multilayer circuits, the pro-
posed Type-II design stands out as the fastest single-layer
multiplier that can be practically implemented. Further-
more, the proposed design II exhibits the smallest area
among all compared designs, achieving a 14% reduction
compared to reference [9]. In addition, it demonstrates
a 1.6% improvement in cell count compared to the best
design in terms of quantum cell consumption [9].

the origin, the more ideal it is, indicating lower delay and
area. Te positions of the proposed Type-I and Type-II
multipliers in this plot clearly demonstrate their superior
circuit parameters. Ultimately, through a comprehensive
comparison, we conclude that the proposed Type-II design is
the fastest and the most optimal design in terms of all three

6. Conclusion
Comparison results between the proposed designs and
previous works demonstrate that the proposed Type-II
design achieved signifcant improvements in delay, area,
and cell count for both two-bit and four-bit implementa-
tions. Given our objective of designing a high-speed single-
layer array multiplier, the Type-II design successfully met
this goal. Specifcally, the Type-II design achieved a 65%
delay reduction, compared to the fastest previous single-
layer two-bit design and a 32.5% delay reduction for the
four-bit case. Tese results establish the Type-II design as the
fastest single-layer two-bit and four-bit multipliers. Future
work should focus on addressing fabrication challenges and
exploring low-power design techniques to further improve
QCA circuit performance. Moreover, all proposed designs
exhibit a regular structure for input and output operations,
making them suitable for quantum computing units,
quantum calculators, quantum flters, and other quantum
circuits.
